messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 72
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Network Engineer
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 36

Martha is a 72-year-old network engineer who has worked for the same telecommunications company for nearly four decades. She is small and wiry, with steady hands that have crimped thousands of Ethernet cables, and a mind that can still visualize an entire fiber-optic backbone without a diagram. Her husband of fifty years, Carl, says she has always been the most organized person he knows. But in the past two years, that organization has become something else—a rigid, brittle scaffolding she clings to.

The event happened twenty-nine months ago, on a Wednesday afternoon in late October. Martha was on the fourteenth floor of the company’s downtown headquarters, running a routine audit of the network closets. She heard shouting from the adjacent corridor, then a crash. When she stepped out, she saw a junior technician, a twenty-three-year-old named Devon, lying at the bottom of an open service elevator shaft. The safety gate had failed while he was checking a cable tray on the mezzanine. Martha did not scream. She knelt beside him, pressed her hands over the wound on his chest, and held his gaze for the three minutes it took for the paramedics to arrive. He died before they lifted him out.

In the weeks that followed, Martha did what she always did: she returned to work, filed the incident report, attended the memorial, and helped redesign the elevator gate protocol. She told herself she was fine. She had seen worse in her career—a colleague electrocuted in the 1980s, a fiber-optic laser accident that blinded a man in one eye. You move on. But this time, moving on did not take.

Now, when Martha walks into the building, she takes the stairs instead of the elevator. She climbs fourteen flights twice a day, her knees aching, because the sight of an open elevator door makes her stomach drop and her heart race. She has told Carl it is for the exercise. He does not argue, but she knows he notices the way she flinches at the creak of the stairwell door, the way she scans every corridor before she enters.

At her desk, she can still do her work—she is the only person who understands the legacy trunk lines from the 1990s—but her concentration fractures easily. A sudden knock on the door sends a jolt through her chest. The whir of a server fan can pull her back to the sound of Devon’s gasp. Several times a week, she finds herself staring at a blank terminal screen, her hands frozen on the keyboard, replaying the wet sound of her palms against his shirt.

She avoids the fourteenth floor entirely. When a project requires her to go there, she delegates the site visit to a junior engineer, making excuses about her back. She has also stopped eating lunch in the break room because the fluorescent lights hum at a frequency that reminds her of the elevator motor. Some days she brings a sandwich and eats it in her car, the doors locked, the radio off.

At home, Martha has become restless. She sleeps in fits, waking several times a night with the sensation of someone falling—a sharp, vertiginous lurch that leaves her gripping the mattress. Carl has suggested she see a doctor, but she waves him off. She is too old for counseling, she says. She has a mind for logic and data, not feelings.

But the feelings are there, buried under the cables and schematics. She has not visited her grandchildren in months because the youngest, a five-year-old, loves to jump off the couch and pretend to fly. The sight makes Martha’s chest tighten. She tells herself she is just tired. She has been a network engineer for forty-six years. She deserves to slow down.

On paper, Martha’s life looks steady. She is married, employed, physically healthy. But inside, she is still on that corridor floor, her hands stained red, waiting for a sound that will not come. The PCL-5 score of 36 reflects what she will not admit: that the memory is no longer a memory. It is the room she lives in.
